Chi-square test of homogeneity for two categorical samples

Source: R/drift.R
drfthomog.Rd

Tests whether two samples of a categorical variable (for example race, offence type or region in an old and a new data extract) were drawn from the same distribution, by Pearson's chi-square on the 2-by-k contingency table of their counts. Use it to ask whether the mix of categories has changed between two samples; it is the categorical test that cpsdrft() runs.

Usage

drfthomog(x, y, seed = 1L)

Arguments

x, y

Factor or character vectors (or named count vectors) – the reference and the new sample.

seed

Integer, default 1: seed for the Monte Carlo branch (small expected counts). The draw is made under this seed and the caller's RNG stream is restored, so the same inputs give the same p-value and nothing downstream moves.

Value

A named length-4 numeric: statistic, df, p_value and logpvalue, the natural log of the upper tail, which keeps its information where p_value underflows to 0. On the Monte Carlo branch (sparse tables) p_value is floored at 1/(B+1) and logpvalue is its log, so it carries no extra range there. The attribute method names the branch, or says why the test was inapplicable (one category, no counts). It has class c("rmbl_drfthomog", "rmbl_measure", "numeric"), so it prints as a box with its inputs (kept in attribute "lakner"); arithmetic, [, c() and as.numeric() give plain numbers.

Details

With pooled shares \(\hat\pi_j = (x_j + y_j)/(n_x + n_y)\) and expected counts \(n_x \hat\pi_j\) and \(n_y \hat\pi_j\), $$X^2 = \sum_j \frac{(x_j - n_x\hat\pi_j)^2}{n_x\hat\pi_j} + \frac{(y_j - n_y\hat\pi_j)^2}{n_y\hat\pi_j}$$ on \(k - 1\) degrees of freedom. Three branches, named in the method attribute:

  • "chi-square approximation": every expected count is at least 5; the p-value is the chi-square upper tail.

  • "Monte Carlo permutation (small expected counts)": some expected count is below 5; the p-value then comes from stats::chisq.test() with simulate.p.value = TRUE and B = 10000 tables with the same margins, drawn under seed.

  • "inapplicable: ...": a single category, or fewer than two observations per category (for example two disjoint sets of dates); no test has power there, so p_value is NA rather than 1.

Errors: a numeric vector without names; negative, infinite or missing counts; an empty sample.

Why this and not drftchisq()

drftchisq() compares observed counts against a distribution taken as KNOWN – proportions fixed by a specification. When the reference is itself a finite sample, that treatment ignores the reference's own sampling error, understates the variance of the comparison, and so reports drift too readily. A homogeneity test estimates the shared distribution from the pooled margins and carries the uncertainty of both samples, which is the right test when comparing a pinned extract with a fresh fetch. cpsdrft() therefore uses this one.

Categories present in only one sample are aligned by name and given zero counts, so an appearing or vanishing level registers.

See also

drftchisq() for a known reference distribution, stats::chisq.test() for the full test object.

Examples

set.seed(1)
a <- sample(c("x", "y", "z"), 300, TRUE)
b <- sample(c("x", "y", "z"), 300, TRUE)

# Two draws from the same distribution: no evidence of a difference.
drfthomog(a, b)
#> ╭── Chi-square test of homogeneity ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Samples     300 and 300 values                                          │
#> │   Categories  3                                                           │
#> │   Method      chi-square approximation                                    │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   statistic  value                                                        │
#> │   ---------  -------                                                      │
#> │   statistic  0.515                                                        │
#> │   df         2                                                            │
#> │   p_value    0.773                                                        │
#> │   logpvalue  -0.2575                                                      │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   The two samples' mixes of categories agree (p = 0.773, not below 0.05). │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   Both samples carry sampling error; with an expected count below 5       │
#> │   the p-value is a Monte Carlo one under a fixed seed.                    │
#> ╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

# A reallocated mix is detected.
drfthomog(a, sample(c("x", "y", "z"), 300, TRUE,
                            prob = c(0.7, 0.2, 0.1)))
#> ╭── Chi-square test of homogeneity ──────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Samples     300 and 300 values                                       │
#> │   Categories  3                                                        │
#> │   Method      chi-square approximation                                 │
#> │                                                                        │
#> │   statistic  value                                                     │
#> │   ---------  -------                                                   │
#> │   statistic  69.78                                                     │
#> │   df         2                                                         │
#> │   p_value    < 0.001                                                   │
#> │   logpvalue  -34.89                                                    │
#> │                                                                        │
#> │   The two samples' mixes of categories differ (p < 0.001, below 0.05). │
#> │                                                                        │
#> │   Both samples carry sampling error; with an expected count below 5    │
#> │   the p-value is a Monte Carlo one under a fixed seed.                 │
#> ╰────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯

# Agrees with stats::chisq.test() on the 2-by-k table.
tab <- rbind(table(a), table(b))
all.equal(drfthomog(a, b)[["statistic"]],
          as.numeric(stats::chisq.test(tab)$statistic))
#> [1] TRUE

# It is more conservative than treating the reference as known, which
# is exactly the point.
drfthomog(a, b)[["p_value"]] >= drftchisq(b, a)[["p_value"]]
#> [1] TRUE

# named count vectors, and a small table that takes the Monte Carlo branch
drfthomog(c(a = 30, b = 20), c(a = 25, b = 25))
#> ╭── Chi-square test of homogeneity ─────────────────────────────────────────╮
#> │   Samples     50 and 50 values                                            │
#> │   Categories  2                                                           │
#> │   Method      chi-square approximation                                    │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   statistic  value                                                        │
#> │   ---------  ------                                                       │
#> │   statistic  1.01                                                         │
#> │   df         1                                                            │
#> │   p_value    0.315                                                        │
#> │   logpvalue  -1.156                                                       │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   The two samples' mixes of categories agree (p = 0.315, not below 0.05). │
#> │                                                                           │
#> │   Both samples carry sampling error; with an expected count below 5       │
#> │   the p-value is a Monte Carlo one under a fixed seed.                    │
#> ╰───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
attr(drfthomog(c(a = 3, b = 1, c = 2), c(a = 1, b = 4, c = 1)), "method")
#> [1] "Monte Carlo permutation (small expected counts)"

try(drfthomog(c(1, 2), c(a = 3)))
#> Error : a numeric `x`/`y` must be named
